title: Training Grants
summary: FIND YOUR LANE → CHECK STATUS → APPLY IN ORDER
subtitle: Most people who miss training money were never turned down. They asked the wrong organization.

blocks.text: Most people who miss training money were never turned down. They asked the only organization they had heard of, got a no, and reasonably concluded the answer was no.
Training money in Canada comes from four separate places, and they barely know each other exists.

The lane you are standing in decides who applies, who receives the money, and whether it arrives before or after you pay tuition. This module sorts the four lanes, shows you how to pitch training to an employer, prices the months you will earn less, and finds the credit that may already be waiting on your tax file.
Finding your lane first can turn a “no” from one office into training you do not pay for alone.
blocks.detail: Who applies, who gets the money and when it arrives all depend on which of four lanes you are in.
blocks.extra: Section 02 helps you find your lane.

sections.title: Four Lanes: Find Yours Before You Do Anything Else

blocks.text: The first question is not what you want to study. It is which lane you are standing in.

items.title: Employed, training for your current job
list: Job Grant programs pay a share of training for an existing employee. The government covers the larger part, the employer the rest.
You cannot apply. Your employer can. Bring a costed proposal, not a request.
Provincially run, and not all running: Ontario’s has been paused for review since late 2025.

items.title: Out of work, or leaving a shrinking industry
list: The largest pot of money in this course, and the least visible, because it has no national brand.
Funded federally, spent provincially under names like Better Jobs Ontario or WorkBC.
Usually needs an eligibility interview. Applying takes weeks, so this lane rewards starting early.

items.title: Paying for your own training
list: Two federal tax tools: the Canada Training Credit and the Lifelong Learning Plan.
Section 04 covers both, with the numbers.

items.title: You are an apprentice
list: A separate system with its own EI rules and an interest-free loan.
The federal apprentice grants ended on March 31, 2025.
The Apprenticeship Funding lesson covers this lane in full.

blocks.text: In lane two, provincial programs can pay tuition, books and a living allowance while you retrain. They are picky, usually want an eligibility interview, and tend to look for a job-market reason rather than a personal interest. New federal measures for apprentices and workers are announced often. Announced is not open. Do not plan a year around a press release.
Canada: Canada Training Credit

sections.title: Lane One: Turn a Request Into a Costed Proposal

blocks.text: In lane one, the useful move is not a form. It is walking into a manager’s office with the program name, the training provider’s quote, and the employer’s share already worked out. Most managers say no to training because it feels like a vague expense. Fewer say no to a costed proposal with most of it already covered.
Here is an example proposal for a program that pays two-thirds of eligible training costs. Check your province’s current share and limits before you use real numbers.
$6,000 of training − $4,000 from the job grant = $2,000 for the employer.
blocks.extra: Your manager is not deciding on $6,000. They are deciding on $2,000, plus your time away from work.

items.title: Total training cost
items.text: Is every cost on the provider’s written quote?

items.title: Course tuition
items.text: Is the provider on the program’s approved list?

items.title: Certification exam
items.text: Does the grant cover exam fees, or only class time?

items.title: Books and materials
items.text: Are these listed as eligible costs?

blocks.text: Add one line about what the business gets: a skill it now buys from a contractor, a licence it needs, or a job it can promote you into instead of hiring from outside. Then hand over the application link. The employer applies, and usually before training starts.

items.title: “My employer would never pay for training.”
items.text: Many employers have never been asked with a number attached. A grant that covers most of the cost changes the question from “can we afford this?” to “can we afford not to?”

sections.title: Lane Three: Paying for Your Own Training

blocks.text: Two federal tools live here, both run through the tax system, and most people who qualify for the first one do not know it exists.
How the Canada Training Credit builds

items.title: Each year
items.text: $250 — added to your limit when you file and qualify, from age 26 to 65.

items.title: Lifetime cap
items.text: $5,000 — the most your limit can ever reach.

items.title: What you claim
items.text: Half — of eligible tuition and fees, up to your limit. You get it even if you owe no tax.

blocks.text: Log into CRA My Account and look at your most recent Notice of Assessment. If you are in the eligible age range and have been filing returns with working income, there may be a Canada training credit limit sitting there, building for years without anyone telling you. The catch: people who stop filing during a low-income stretch stop building it, and those are often the people who later need to retrain. File every year, even a year with almost no income.

items.title: Your Notice of Assessment may already hold training money.
items.text: Your Notice of Assessment may already hold training money.

items.title: Don’t bridge a training gap with high-interest debt.
items.text: Don’t bridge a training gap with high-interest debt.

blocks.text: The Lifelong Learning Plan lets you withdraw from your own RRSP to fund full-time training for yourself or a spouse, tax-free at the time you take it out, with a repayment schedule afterward. It is not free money. It is your own money, borrowed from your future, with lost investment growth as the real cost.

items.title: Canada Training Credit
list: You do not repay it
Arrives after you file, the spring after you pay tuition
Real cost: none, beyond a smaller tuition credit for the same fees

items.title: Lifelong Learning Plan
list: You repay it on a set schedule, or it becomes taxable income
Cash up front, before you enrol
Real cost: lost investment growth, plus repayment pressure

items.title: “Nobody is going to fund a course that is not a full diploma.”
items.text: The Canada Training Credit covers eligible tuition and fees, including many short work courses and licensing programs, not only degrees. Provincial job grants often pay for a few days of certification. The bias toward long programs is in our heads, not in the rules.

sections.title: Price the Months, Not Just the Tuition

blocks.text: The tuition is rarely what sinks a career change. The months without full income are. Before enrolling, work out one figure: the months of reduced income, multiplied by the gap between what you will bring in during training and what your fixed costs need. Then compare it with savings, a partner’s income, a living allowance or EI if you qualify while in approved training.
If the number is uncomfortable, the answer is usually not to give up the plan. It is to change its shape. Here is the same certificate taken two ways.
One certificate, two shapes

items.title: Full time, 8 months
items.text: Monthly shortfall $1,100. Total shortfall $8,800. Tuition $4,000.

items.title: Part time, 18 months
items.text: Monthly shortfall $300. Total shortfall $5,400. Tuition $4,200.

items.title: Difference
items.text: Monthly shortfall $800 lower. Total shortfall $3,400 lower. Tuition $200 higher.

blocks.text: Part time takes longer, but it keeps more of your paycheque and cuts the total gap. A short certification that moves you sideways into a better-paying role first is another shape worth pricing.

People who take on high-interest debt to bridge a training period often finish the program and start the new job already behind. The credential was fine. The financing was the problem. If the gap needs a credit card, change the shape before you enrol.

items.title: “Full time is always the faster way to a better job.”
items.text: Faster to finish, maybe. But a gap you cannot cover can force you to drop out, which is the slowest way of all.

sections.title: What to Do, in What Order

items.title: Check your Notice of Assessment first
items.text: It takes two minutes and tells you what you already have.

items.title: Establish whether the program is open today
items.text: Two federal apprenticeship grants closed in 2025, and at least one large provincial job grant is paused. Search the program name plus the current year and read the official page, not a summary.

items.title: Identify who has to apply
items.text: If it is your employer, your task is persuasion and paperwork preparation, not an application form.

items.title: Book the provincial appointment early if you need one
items.text: Eligibility assessments take weeks, and courses have start dates that do not wait.

items.title: Confirm the training provider qualifies before you pay a deposit
items.text: Most programs only pay for recognized schools or approved provider lists. A deposit paid to a school that does not qualify is gone for good.

items.title: Keep the receipts, and tell your tax preparer what you took
items.text: The training credit is claimed on the return, and nobody claims it for you.

items.title: “I will just enrol now and sort out the funding once I have started.”
items.text: Provincial retraining programs usually will not pay for a course you have already started, and several want the eligibility check first. Tax credits do not care about the order, but everything else in this module does.

sections.title: Marcus, the College Website, and the Question Nobody Asked Him

blocks.text: Marcus and the college website
paragraphs: Marcus is forty-four and drove a delivery route in Regina for eleven years, until his back stopped cooperating with the loading. His goal is a desk job that pays the mortgage. He picks a dispatch and logistics certificate at a local college.
He looks at the tuition on a Sunday night. Then he does what most people do, which is nothing, for four months.

When he finally calls the college’s aid office, they are helpful and tell him about student loans. That is the answer a college gives, because it is the answer a college has. He fills in a loan form, feels worse about the whole thing and stalls again.

A few weeks later, he drops into an employment centre to ask about something else. He almost leaves without mentioning school. Then he decides to ask one more question: is there any help for someone like me?

The counsellor does not ask what he wants to study. She asks if he is working, and if he is leaving a physical job for medical reasons. Both answers put him in a lane he never knew existed. Provincial retraining support will cover his tuition and pay a small allowance while he studies.
There is one more surprise. She tells him to check his Notice of Assessment. He finds a training credit limit that has been building since his thirties.
Marcus cancels the loan application. He had not asked the wrong question. He had asked the right question of an office that could only ever give him one answer.

items.title: COLLEGE AID OFFICE
items.text: Only a loan on offer

items.title: EMPLOYMENT CENTRE
items.text: Retraining lane found

items.title: NOTICE OF ASSESSMENT
items.text: Credit already waiting

blocks.text: Marcus got his tuition covered, and found a credit he never knew he had, by asking one more office one more question.
blocks.detail: Knowing your lane can turn a loan you dread into training that is paid for.
blocks.extra: The quick check in Section 08 tests the math.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: You are employed and want training for your current job. Who applies for a job grant?
items.detail: Your employer. Your job is to bring a costed proposal.

items.title: Training costs $9,000 and a job grant covers two-thirds. What is the employer’s share?
Tuition is $4,000 and your Canada training credit limit is $1,500. What can you claim?
items.detail: $1,500. You can claim half the fees, $2,000, but only up to your limit.

items.title: How fast does the Canada training credit limit build?
items.detail: $250 a year when you file and qualify, to a lifetime cap of $5,000.

items.title: A full-time program leaves you $900 short each month for 10 months. What is the total gap?
items.detail: $9,000. Compare that with savings, an allowance or EI before you enrol.

items.title: A federal program was announced last month. Can you budget for it?
items.detail: Not yet. Check that it is officially open and who qualifies first.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Your Lane

blocks.text: This week: log into CRA My Account and find your Canada training credit limit. Then call or visit your province’s employment services office and ask one question: given my situation, which programs am I eligible to be assessed for? If you are employed, price the training and find your province’s job grant before you talk to your manager. If you cannot say which lane you are in yet, start there.
Four lanes, and the lane decides everything.
blocks.detail: Job grants your employer applies for, provincial retraining programs, tax tools you claim yourself and the separate apprenticeship system. Check your Notice of Assessment first, price the months as well as the tuition, and never assume the first office you called had the whole picture.

items.title: Canada Training Credit
items.text: A refundable federal credit that builds up each year on your tax file and is used against eligible tuition and fees.

items.title: Lifelong Learning Plan
items.text: A tax-free RRSP withdrawal to pay for full-time training, paid back on a set schedule.

items.title: Job Grant
items.text: Provincial programs that pay for training an employer buys for its staff. The employer applies, not the employee.

items.title: Labour Market Transfer Agreements
items.text: The federal-provincial deals that pay for most retraining programs. That is why the money is federal and the program name is provincial.

items.title: Canada Apprentice Loan
items.text: Interest-free borrowing for registered apprentices during school training, available before an EI claim is processed.

items.title: Red Seal trade
items.text: A trade with a national standard and a certificate recognized across provinces. Many apprenticeship supports are limited to these.

items.title: Notice of Assessment
items.text: The CRA summary you get after you file. It shows your training credit limit.

items.title: WHERE TO GET HELP
list: CRA My Account: to check your Canada Training Credit limit, and to file the return that keeps it building.
Your province’s employment services office: for job grants and retraining eligibility assessments.
The Canada Apprentice Loan program: for apprenticeship financing, applied for separately from an EI claim.
Your training provider’s financial aid office: useful for provider questions, but not the place to search for funding.

blocks.text: Program status and provincial rules in this field change often. The Canada Training Credit figures here have been the same since the credit began. Confirm every figure on the program’s own page the day you need it.
